title: Decide FBA vs FBM, and confirm the product is the brand's own, before opening an Amazon account
hypothesis: If we choose FBA or FBM based on the product's size, weight and fragility before opening the account, then early fee and service mistakes fall because the model sets every downstream fee line.
does_not_apply_when: store plans retail arbitrage or wholesale reselling of other brands' products

signal.check: No documented FBA vs FBM decision exists yet for the product going onto Amazon.

expected_effect.size: unknown, avoids rework from picking the wrong fulfilment model

risk.note: Switching models later costs relisting and inventory moves, but making the decision itself carries no risk.

prerequisites: product spec: dimensions, weight, fragility, order volume
steps: List the product's size, weight, fragility and expected monthly order volume.
Decide FBA for a standard, non-fragile product or FBM for a heavy, fragile, low-volume or made-to-order product.
Confirm the product is the brand's own and not resold or arbitraged stock.
Write the decision and the reason in the brand record before opening the account.

test.method: Compare fee totals and service outcomes for FBA vs FBM on this product using the fee model.

title: Default to FBA for standard-size products; model FBM only for heavy, fragile or made-to-order goods
hypothesis: If we default new standard-size products to FBA and only model FBM for exceptions, then Prime eligibility and delivery speed improve because most products fit FBA's size tiers.

signal.check: The product fits a standard FBA size tier but the brand has not modelled FBA against FBM on its own numbers.

expected_effect.size: unknown, avoid assuming a fixed sales multiplier from FBA

risk.note: Modelling both takes an afternoon; the risk is assuming a fixed FBA sales multiplier without checking the brand's own contribution margin.

prerequisites: fee and margin model output for both FBA and FBM
steps: List exceptions: heavy, fragile, low-volume or made-to-order.
If none apply, default to FBA.
Model contribution margin and conversion for both FBA and FBM rather than assuming a fixed multiplier.
Record the choice and the numbers behind it.

test.method: Compare conversion rate and contribution margin for FBA vs FBM once live.

title: Gate adding Amazon on the brand's own landed cost and price, not on course figures
hypothesis: If we run the unit economics gate on the brand's real landed cost and price before adding Amazon, then wasted launch spend falls because a bad-margin SKU is caught before stock ships.

signal.check: No margin model has been run on the brand's own landed cost and price for the Amazon-bound SKU.

expected_effect.size: unknown, avoids launching a SKU that cannot clear a 30% net margin gate

risk.note: Running the gate has no downside; skipping it risks a launch that never turns a profit.

steps: Pull the brand's landed cost per unit and target sell price.
Run the fee and margin model on those numbers, not on a course's example figures.
Check the result against the 30% net margin gate.
Stop or fix the product if the gate fails.

test.method: Run the margin model before and after any cost or price change and compare against the 30% gate.
test.read_point: before committing to a first production run

title: Build the Amazon launch budget from line items, not a single headline number
hypothesis: If we build the launch budget line by line (stock, freight, fees, tools, trademark, PPC) instead of using one headline figure, then cash shortfalls mid-launch fall because every cost is accounted for in advance.

signal.check: The brand has a single lump-sum launch budget with no line-item breakdown.

expected_effect.size: unknown, reduces the chance of running out of cash mid-launch

risk.note: Building a detailed budget has no downside beyond the time it takes.

steps: List every line: stock, freight, duty, GS1, trademark, samples, inspection, packaging, photos, PPC reserve, plan fee, cushion.
Get a real quote or brand figure for each line instead of a course's example number.
Sum the lines into a launch budget and compare against cash on hand.
Flag any line still unknown as a web check or a quote to chase.

test.method: Compare actual spend against the line-item budget once the launch is underway.
test.read_point: at launch and again at 30 days

title: Match the target Amazon revenue band to the cash the brand actually has available
hypothesis: If we size the target Amazon revenue band to available cash instead of the biggest opportunity, then the launch stays funded because inventory and ad spend never outrun the cash on hand.

signal.check: The brand is targeting a monthly revenue figure without checking it against cash for 3 months of stock plus a PPC reserve.

expected_effect.size: unknown, keeps the launch inside the brand's real cash limit

risk.note: None; this is a planning check, not a spending change.

prerequisites: cash available for inventory and ads
steps: State the cash available for the first order and 3 months of PPC.
Pick a revenue band the brand can fund at that level, even a smaller one.
Avoid chasing a bigger revenue band than the cash supports.

test.method: Track whether cash on hand covers stock and PPC through the planned window without a gap.
test.read_point: before placing the first production order

title: Set a launch date once the product clears the price, margin and differentiation gates; stop re-researching
hypothesis: If we set a firm launch date once the gates pass instead of continuing to research, then lost revenue from delay falls because extra research after the gates pass adds cost, not new information.
does_not_apply_when: a real supply-chain problem still needs solving, in which case fix the supplier first

signal.check: The product has passed the price, margin and differentiation gates but no launch date is set and research continues.

expected_effect.size: unknown, avoids the cost of open-ended delay after the gates pass

risk.note: Launching before the gates pass is the real risk; this idea only applies once they have passed.

prerequisites: gates passed: price, margin, differentiation, supplier acceptable
steps: Confirm the product passed the price, margin and differentiation gates.
Confirm the supplier is acceptable.
Set a launch date and work backward from it.
Treat any further delay as a cost, not more research.

test.method: Track months from gate-pass to launch date across products and compare to estimated delay cost.

title: Reject a product that cannot win a price or review fight against the top 10 listings
hypothesis: If we reject a generic clone unless it names one fixable gap from competitor reviews, then failed launches fall because generic private label loses on price or reviews against an established top 10.

signal.check: The shortlisted product is a close copy of the top 10 listings with no named fixable complaint from their reviews.

expected_effect.size: unknown, avoids launching into a fight the product cannot win

risk.note: None; this is a screen before spending on stock.

prerequisites: review mining of top 10 competitors (see idea on mining 1-3 star reviews)
steps: Read the top 10 listings' 1 to 3 star reviews.
Name one specific, fixable gap the product will close.
If no gap exists, reject or change the product before ordering stock.

test.method: Track win rate: launches with a named fixable gap vs launches without one, by first-90-day sell-through.
test.read_point: before committing to a production run

title: Model Seller Fulfilled Prime as an FBM alternative when the brand can meet Prime delivery standards itself
hypothesis: If we model Seller Fulfilled Prime for a heavy, fragile or low-volume SKU the brand can ship fast and reliably itself, then the brand can keep the Prime badge and control while avoiding FBA fees on that SKU.
does_not_apply_when: brand cannot meet Prime delivery speed and cancellation-rate standards

signal.check: A heavy, fragile or low-volume SKU is being defaulted to FBM without checking whether SFP is available and worthwhile.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no source gives SFP enrolment steps or standards

risk.note: Missing a Prime delivery or cancellation standard can suspend SFP status; verify current standards before enrolling.

prerequisites: web check on current SFP standards
steps: Check whether the SKU is a poor fit for FBA (heavy, fragile, low-volume).
Look up current Seller Fulfilled Prime standards and eligibility.
Model the cost of meeting SFP delivery and cancellation standards against FBA and plain FBM.
Enrol only if the brand can consistently meet the standards.

test.method: Track on-time ship rate and cancellation rate against SFP's required thresholds after enrolling.

title: Choose the Professional plan above about 40 units a month expected; stay on Individual below that
hypothesis: If we pick the Professional or Individual plan based on the ~40 unit a month breakeven instead of guessing, then fixed plan cost falls because low-volume sellers avoid paying a flat monthly fee they don't need.

signal.check: Expected monthly units and the current plan choice have not been compared against the breakeven point.

expected_effect.size: unknown, avoids overpaying the Professional fee at low volume

risk.note: Switching plans later is straightforward, so this is low risk either way.

prerequisites: web check on current plan prices
steps: Estimate expected units per month at go-live.
Check the live Professional plan price and the per-item Individual fee.
Compute the breakeven units for the current fees.
Choose Professional above breakeven, Individual below it, and avoid paying Professional during pre-launch research.

test.method: Compare actual monthly units against the breakeven point after the first 2 months live.

title: Disclose any existing or previously suspended Amazon seller account before opening a new one
hypothesis: If we disclose any prior or suspended Amazon account at signup, then account rejection and suspension risk falls because an undisclosed duplicate account is a top cause of both.

signal.check: Anyone involved in the new account has ever had an Amazon seller account, active or suspended, that has not been disclosed.

expected_effect.size: unknown, undisclosed prior accounts are a named rejection cause

risk.note: A duplicate, undisclosed account can get both accounts suspended; disclosure is the only fix once one exists.

prerequisites: ask everyone with signing authority about any past Amazon seller account
steps: Ask everyone involved in the account about any past Amazon seller account, even a forgotten one.
Disclose any prior or suspended account to Amazon during signup.
Never open a second account without telling Amazon first.

test.method: Track whether the account clears verification without a duplicate-account flag.

title: Gather the full identity, bank and tax document set and register under a name matching ID exactly
hypothesis: If we gather the full document set and match the registered name to ID and proof of address exactly before starting signup, then verification delays fall because mismatches are the main cause of holdups.

signal.check: Signup is starting without government ID, a downloaded bank statement PDF, proof of address, tax ID and payment card gathered in advance.

expected_effect.size: unknown, avoids delay from document mismatches

risk.note: None; this is preparation before signup.

steps: List the required documents: government ID, downloaded bank statement PDF, proof of address, bank details, tax ID, phone, business email, payment card.
Check every document uses the exact same registered name.
Gather all documents before starting the signup flow.
Confirm current requirements with a live check before submitting.

test.method: Track days from signup start to verified account.

title: Use a business credit card, not a debit or prepaid card, when opening the Amazon seller account
hypothesis: If we use a business credit card at signup instead of a debit or prepaid card, then the chance of a payment-related account flag falls because a credit card is the stricter, safer option across sources that disagree.

signal.check: The account signup form is about to be completed and no payment card has been chosen yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown, sources disagree on whether debit works; credit is the strict choice

risk.note: One source reports a debit card working; treat the suspension claim as unverified either way.

steps: Get a business credit card before starting signup, if the brand does not already have one.
Use it as the payment method during account setup.
Keep it separate from personal spend for cleaner bookkeeping.

test.method: Track whether the account clears verification without a payment-related flag.

title: Prepare for Amazon's live video identity verification call with matching ID and a utility bill on hand
hypothesis: If we prepare the same ID used on the application and have a utility bill ready before the video call, then added verification delay falls because a data mismatch is the main cause of the up to 48 hour extra wait.

signal.check: A video verification call is scheduled or expected and the exact ID and address documents have not been checked against the application.

expected_effect.size: unknown, presenter reports up to 48 hours added per mismatch

risk.note: None; this is preparation, not a change to the account.

prerequisites: document set from the signup prep idea
steps: Confirm the exact ID used matches the application data (name, birthdate, address).
Have a recent utility bill ready in case proof of address is requested.
Do not record the call; join from a quiet, well-lit space.
Keep the same ID in hand for the whole call.

test.method: Track hours from call to verified status.

title: Do not change bank details or business address for 1 to 2 months after account approval
hypothesis: If we hold off changing bank details or business address for 1 to 2 months after approval, then account review risk falls because Amazon reads early changes as a fraud signal in at least one source.

signal.check: The account was approved within the last 2 months and a bank or address change is being considered.

expected_effect.size: unknown, single-source claim, treat as a precaution

risk.note: Delaying a needed change by a few weeks is a minor inconvenience against an account review risk.

steps: Make any planned bank or address change before signup, not after.
If a change is unavoidable in the first 1 to 2 months, expect possible extra review.
Document the reason for any early change in the account record.

test.method: Track whether any early account change triggers a review or hold.

title: Add payout bank details and pass verification before sourcing or shipping any stock
hypothesis: If we confirm payout bank details and verification are done before placing a production order, then cash flow risk falls because a blocked payout would leave revenue stuck with stock already committed.

signal.check: A production order is being planned and payout bank verification is not yet confirmed complete.

expected_effect.size: unknown, sequencing check

risk.note: None; this is a sequencing check before spending on stock.

steps: Confirm payout bank details are entered and verified in Seller Central.
Confirm no pending document requests remain.
Only then place the production order or book freight.

test.method: Track whether payout verification is complete before the first shipment leaves the factory.

title: Open the Amazon account under a business entity with its own EIN and bank account before the first sale
hypothesis: If we open the Amazon account under a dedicated business entity with its own EIN and bank account, then payout verification mismatches fall because a personal-account mismatch is a common block.

signal.check: The Amazon account is being opened under a personal name and bank account rather than a registered business entity.

expected_effect.size: unknown, avoids a personal vs business mismatch at verification

risk.note: Entity setup takes time and a small fee; route the entity type decision itself to the finance track.

prerequisites: route entity choice to finance and accounting
steps: Confirm the brand has a registered business entity with its own EIN.
Open a business bank account under that entity.
Use the entity's EIN and bank account when signing up for Amazon.
Check current sales tax nexus and marketplace facilitator rules before the first sale.

test.method: Track whether payout verification passes without a name or entity mismatch.

title: Buy UPC barcodes from GS1 directly, never from gray-market resellers
hypothesis: If we buy UPCs from GS1 instead of a reseller, then listing and account suspension risk from barcode mismatches falls because reseller codes sometimes fail Amazon's checks.

signal.check: A new ASIN needs a UPC and the current plan is to buy one from a reseller instead of GS1.

expected_effect.size: unknown, reseller codes are flagged as a listing and account risk

risk.note: GS1 costs more per code than a reseller, but avoids a listing or account problem later.

steps: Get a current price check on GS1 UPCs.
Buy the UPC directly from GS1 for the new ASIN.
Avoid gray-market or reseller barcode sources even if cheaper.

test.method: Track whether the ASIN lists and stays listed without a barcode-related flag.

title: Add VAT to the Amazon fee lines before judging margin on UK or EU sales
hypothesis: If we add VAT on Amazon's selling and fulfilment fees to the margin model, then the margin gate reads correctly because the standard fee calculator does not show this VAT by default in at least one marketplace.
does_not_apply_when: marketplace is not one where VAT applies to Amazon's own fees

signal.check: The margin model for a UK or EU listing does not include VAT on Amazon's selling and fulfilment fees.

expected_effect.size: about 20% VAT added to Amazon's fee lines in one source's example

risk.note: None; this corrects a margin calculation, it does not change any live setting.

prerequisites: current VAT treatment for the marketplace
steps: Check the live VAT rule on Amazon fees for the target marketplace.
Add that VAT rate to the referral and fulfilment fee lines in the margin model.
Re-check the 30% net margin gate with VAT included.

test.method: Compare the margin model's predicted net margin against the actual settlement report once live.
test.read_point: before launch and after the first settlement

title: File a trademark application before or at listing creation, do not wait for approval
hypothesis: If we file the trademark application before or at listing creation instead of waiting for approval, then Brand Registry enrolment starts months sooner because the application number alone is enough to enrol.

signal.check: The brand sells its own branded product on Amazon and has not yet filed a trademark application.

expected_effect.size: 6 to 18 months of approval lag avoided by enrolling on the application number

risk.note: DIY filing fees are quoted inconsistently across sources; get a live fee check and consider a lawyer add-on for a stronger filing.

steps: Screen the brand name for trademark conflicts.
Choose the mark type (design or word).
File at USPTO or the relevant IP office with a live fee check.
Record the application serial number in the brand record.
Enrol in Brand Registry using the application number once a listing exists.

test.method: Track days from filing to Brand Registry enrolment.
test.read_point: at filing and again at enrolment

title: Choose a design (logo) mark over a word mark when the brand name sits on the listing image and packaging
hypothesis: If we file a design mark instead of a word mark when the name appears as a logo on packaging, then the risk of a denied filing forcing a rebrand falls because a word mark is harder to win in that situation.
does_not_apply_when: the brand name itself, in plain text, is the only mark being used with no logo styling

signal.check: The brand name is styled as a logo on the product image and packaging but the trademark filing plan uses a word mark.

expected_effect.size: one reported case of 100,000 dollars plus opportunity cost from a denied word mark forcing a rebrand

risk.note: A denied word mark stalls Brand Registry, A+, Sponsored Brands and hijacker protection on the ASIN, not just the trademark itself.

steps: Check whether the brand name is used as a styled logo on the listing image and packaging.
If so, file a design mark covering that logo instead of a plain word mark.
Confirm the choice with trademark counsel before filing.

test.method: Track approval outcome (approved, denied, or opposed) by mark type.

title: Create the product listing before applying for Brand Registry, since enrolment needs an ASIN
hypothesis: If we create the listing, even an imperfect one, before applying for Brand Registry, then enrolment is not blocked because the program requires an existing ASIN to attach the trademark to.

signal.check: A trademark application exists but no product listing has been created yet, blocking Brand Registry enrolment.

expected_effect.size: unknown, removes a sequencing block on enrolment

risk.note: The listing can be imperfect and improved later; the point is to have an ASIN to enrol.

prerequisites: trademark application filed or in progress
steps: Confirm the trademark application exists.
Create the product listing, even a basic first version.
Apply for Brand Registry once the ASIN and application number both exist.

test.method: Track days from trademark filing to a live ASIN to Brand Registry enrolment.

title: Record the trademark application serial number in the brand record right after filing
hypothesis: If we record the trademark serial number in the brand record immediately after filing, then Brand Registry enrolment moves faster because the number is ready when the listing goes live instead of being tracked down later.

signal.check: A trademark has been filed but the serial number is not yet stored anywhere in the brand record.

expected_effect.size: unknown, removes a lookup delay at enrolment

risk.note: None; this is a recordkeeping step.

steps: File the trademark application.
Copy the application serial number into the brand record the same day.
Reference that record when enrolling in Brand Registry.

test.method: Check the brand record has the serial number on file before Brand Registry enrolment starts.

title: Enrol in Brand Registry as soon as eligible and turn on its benefits
hypothesis: If we enrol in Brand Registry as soon as eligible and turn on A+ content, Transparency and Attribution, then listing conversion and hijacker protection improve because these benefits are unavailable before enrolment.

signal.check: The brand is eligible for Brand Registry (trademark filed, ASIN live) but has not enrolled.

expected_effect.size: unknown, A+ content and other benefits are source-claimed conversion levers, not measured here

risk.note: Program terms and benefit lists change; verify current benefits before promising them to a client.

steps: Confirm trademark application number and a live ASIN exist.
Enrol at Brand Registry using both.
Turn on A+ content once approved.
Set up Transparency if hijack risk exists, and review Brand Analytics.

test.method: Compare conversion rate and hijacker incidents before and after enrolment.

title: Track Brand Referral Bonus with tracked Attribution links; do not assume a fixed percentage back
hypothesis: If we track external traffic to the Amazon listing with Attribution links and reconcile the actual bonus paid, then off-Amazon acquisition cost reads correctly because the sources disagree on whether the bonus is 15 percent falling to 5 percent or about 10 percent back.

signal.check: The brand sends email, social or ad traffic to its Amazon listing without a tracked Attribution link or a reconciliation of the credit received.

expected_effect.size: unknown, sources give two different bonus framings

risk.note: None; this is a measurement fix.

steps: Enrol in the Brand Referral Bonus program through Brand Registry.
Create tracked Attribution links for every off-Amazon channel sending traffic to the listing.
Reconcile the actual credited amount each month instead of assuming a fixed percentage.

test.method: Compare tracked external sales against the Brand Referral Bonus credited in the account.

title: Get a lawyer-reviewed NNN agreement before a production PO to an overseas factory
hypothesis: If we get an NNN agreement reviewed by counsel before the first production PO, then the risk of a factory copying or leaking the design falls because a Western NDA is reported as weak protection in that country.
does_not_apply_when: product is sourced domestically with no overseas manufacturing

signal.check: A production purchase order is planned with an overseas factory for a novel product and no NNN agreement has been reviewed by counsel.

expected_effect.size: unknown, legal opinion only, not measured

risk.note: This is legal advice territory; verify the NNN claim and any patent filing with qualified counsel, not the playbook.

steps: Engage counsel experienced in the manufacturing country.
Have counsel draft or review an NNN agreement with the factory.
Sign the NNN agreement before the production PO.
Budget a provisional patent filing in the launch budget if the product is novel.

test.method: Confirm the NNN agreement is signed and filed before the PO is placed.

title: Enrol a repeat-purchase product in Subscribe & Save once Brand Registered, modelled into the margin gate
hypothesis: If we enrol a consumable or repeat-purchase SKU in Subscribe & Save and model the subscriber discount into the margin gate first, then repeat purchase rate rises without breaking the 30% net margin gate.
does_not_apply_when: product is not consumable or repeat-purchase
brand is not yet Brand Registered

signal.check: A consumable or steady-repeat product is Brand Registered but not enrolled in Subscribe & Save.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no source gives the discount mechanics

risk.note: Model the subscriber discount into the margin gate first so Subscribe & Save does not quietly erase profit.

steps: Confirm the product is consumable or has steady repeat demand.
Model the Subscribe & Save discount into the 30% net margin gate.
Enrol the ASIN in Subscribe & Save once the margin still clears.
Watch repeat purchase rate after enrolling.

test.method: Compare repeat purchase rate and net margin before and after enrolling in Subscribe & Save.

title: Build a Brand Registry Storefront as a destination for off-Amazon and Sponsored Brands traffic
hypothesis: If we build a Storefront once Brand Registered and route Sponsored Brands and off-Amazon traffic to it, then conversion on that traffic improves because it lands on a fuller brand page instead of a single listing.
does_not_apply_when: brand has only one ASIN and no brand story to tell

signal.check: The brand is Brand Registered with more than one ASIN or a story to tell, but has no Storefront built.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no source gives structure or a measured result

risk.note: None; a Storefront does not replace the product listing itself.

steps: Confirm Brand Registry is active.
Build a Storefront with the brand's story and product range.
Route Sponsored Brands clicks and off-Amazon links to the Storefront where it fits the campaign.
Review Storefront traffic and conversion monthly.

test.method: Compare conversion rate of Storefront-routed traffic against listing-only traffic.

title: Screen out disqualifying products first: cheap, head-on competitive, seasonal or restricted
hypothesis: If we run the elimination screen before judging upside on any candidate, then wasted research time falls because a disqualifying flaw is cheaper to catch early than after a full research pass.

signal.check: A candidate product is being researched in depth before checking it against the disqualifying list.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a screening step, not a measured outcome

risk.note: None; this is a first-pass filter before spending research time.

steps: Check the product against the elimination list: too cheap, seasonal or trend, restricted, gated, patented, or head-on competitive.
Check the live restricted and gated category list.
Drop the candidate immediately if any flag applies.
Only continue researching candidates that clear this screen.

test.method: Track the share of candidates dropped at this stage vs later, more expensive stages.

title: Target a sell price of $25 or more for a new launch; treat $15 as the floor and discard under about $10
hypothesis: If we target $25 or more for a new Amazon launch and discard anything under about $10, then per-click PPC cost stops erasing profit because cheap items lose margin in 2 to 3 clicks.

signal.check: The candidate product's likely sell price is under $25 and has not been checked against the price floor rule.

expected_effect.size: unknown, presenter heuristic from two sources on the price floor

risk.note: A strong reason (very low FBA fee tier, high repeat rate) can justify $15 to $25 if the margin gate still clears.

steps: Estimate the likely competitive sell price for the product.
Discard candidates likely to sell under about $10.
Treat $15 as the firm floor and $25 or more as the target.
Re-check the 30% net margin gate at the chosen price.

test.method: Compare margin and PPC efficiency across launched SKUs by price band.

title: Require both real demand and low competition before shortlisting a product
hypothesis: If we require high search demand together with weak existing listings before shortlisting a product, then launch failure rate falls because either factor alone (demand with no room, or low competition with no demand) predicts a weak launch.

signal.check: A candidate shows strong demand or weak competition but has not been checked for both together.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a screening step

risk.note: None; a screening check.

steps: Check search volume for the product's core keyword.
Check the review counts of the top sellers for that keyword.
Shortlist only if volume is high and top-seller review counts are low.
Drop candidates missing either factor.

test.method: Track first-90-day sell-through by whether both factors were present at screening.

title: Reject categories dominated by 1 or 2 legacy brands
hypothesis: If we reject a category where 1 or 2 legacy brands take most of the sales, then launch failure rate falls because a new own-brand product rarely displaces an entrenched leader on trust alone.

signal.check: The top sellers for the target keyword are dominated by 1 or 2 well-known legacy brands.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no numeric threshold given by either source

risk.note: None; a screening check.

steps: List the brands selling on page 1 for the core keyword.
Check whether 1 or 2 brands account for most of the visible sales.
Drop the candidate if a small number of legacy brands dominate.

test.method: Track first-90-day sell-through against category brand concentration at screening.

title: Reject a product with a tight page-1 price cluster; prefer a wide legitimate price spread
hypothesis: If we reject products where page-1 prices cluster tightly and prefer a wide spread, then pricing power improves because a tight cluster means buyers pick on price and stars alone.

signal.check: The top 10 listings for the target keyword sell within a narrow price band.

expected_effect.size: example spreads: tight $7 to $13 vs wide $20 to $100 on the same search page

risk.note: None; a screening check.

steps: Record the prices of the top 10 listings for the target keyword.
Check whether the spread is wide (legitimate differences buyers pay for) or tight (a price and star-rating fight).
Prefer or reposition toward a wide-spread category; drop a tight-cluster candidate.

test.method: Track achieved price and margin against the page-1 spread recorded at screening.

title: Prefer products with many distinct search phrasings over one or two monolithic terms
hypothesis: If we prefer a product with dozens of distinct search phrasings, then cheap long-tail entry becomes available because a product with only 1 or 2 monolithic terms forces one expensive, contested battle.

signal.check: The candidate product is searched mainly through 1 or 2 dominant phrases with no long-tail variation.

expected_effect.size: unknown, presenter reasoning on long-tail entry cost

risk.note: None; a screening check.

steps: List distinct ways shoppers search for the product (material, size, use case, audience).
Count the distinct phrasings with real search volume.
Deprioritise a candidate with only 1 or 2 monolithic terms.

test.method: Track PPC cost per click across launched SKUs against keyword variability at screening.

title: Require at least 8 months of listing age on comparable products before treating demand as evergreen
hypothesis: If we require comparable listings to be at least 8 months old before trusting their revenue as evergreen demand, then fad-driven launches fall because newer listings can be riding a trend that fades before stock arrives.

signal.check: The comparable listings used to validate demand for a candidate are younger than 8 months old.

expected_effect.size: presenter filter: 8 months minimum listing age

risk.note: None; a screening check.

steps: Check the first-available date of the comparable listings used for demand validation.
Treat listings under 8 months old as fad risk, not proven demand.
Re-validate demand with older comparables before committing.

test.method: Track whether launches validated on 8+ month comparables held sales past month 6 more often than ones that were not.

title: Mine 1-star to 3-star reviews of selling competitors and write each fixable complaint into the product brief
hypothesis: If we mine competitors' 1 to 3 star reviews and turn each recurring fixable complaint into a product brief line, then differentiation improves because the product launches already solving a named, proven pain point.

signal.check: A candidate product has not had its top competitors' negative reviews read for recurring, fixable complaints.

expected_effect.size: example: 12% share of 1-star reviews used as an opportunity signal in one source

risk.note: None; this is a research step feeding the product brief.

steps: Open the top selling competitors' listings.
Sort or filter to 1 to 3 star reviews.
Note the share of 1-star reviews and any recurring, fixable complaint.
Write each fixable complaint into the product brief as a design or spec requirement.

test.method: Track the product's own review rating and complaint themes after launch against the briefed fixes.

title: Treat a 4.1 to 4.3 star competitor doing $5,000 or more a month as proof of demand with a spec gap
hypothesis: If we treat a mid-rated, high-revenue competitor as proof of demand rather than a threat, then product selection improves because that rating band signals real sales with a fixable quality gap.

signal.check: A candidate category has a competitor rated 4.1 to 4.3 stars doing an estimated $5,000 or more a month, but it has not been logged as a demand-proof signal.

expected_effect.size: presenter pattern: 4.1 to 4.3 stars plus $5,000+ a month

risk.note: None; a screening pattern to look for, not a guarantee.

steps: Sort competitor results by rating, low to high.
Find competitors rated 4.1 to 4.3 stars with an estimated $5,000+ a month in revenue.
Read their reviews for the fixable gap driving the mid rating.
Log this as proof of demand for the category.

test.method: Track how often this pattern predicted a successful launch across candidates.

title: Run two different product-research filter recipes as separate passes, not copy one verbatim
hypothesis: If we run two different research tool filter recipes as separate, labelled passes, then the product shortlist improves because copying one presenter's exact filters surfaces the same products everyone else already finds.

signal.check: Product research is using only one presenter's exact filter values (price, revenue, rating, review count) with no variation.

expected_effect.size: unknown, presenter's own warning against copying filters verbatim

risk.note: None; this changes which candidates surface, not a live setting.

steps: Run a first pass with one filter recipe (for example price $15-85, revenue $5,000-80,000, max rating 3.5).
Run a second pass with a different recipe (for example reviews max 300, price $25-60, revenue $5,000-20,000, age 8+ months, images max 4).
Label which recipe found each candidate.
Pass a candidate only if the manual checks (price spread, brand dominance, keyword variability, review mining) also pass.

test.method: Track how many shortlisted candidates came from each recipe and how they performed after launch.

title: Validate a keyword gap live on Amazon search, not only inside the research tool
hypothesis: If we confirm a keyword volume-with-no-listing gap by searching it live on Amazon, then wasted product bets on a false gap fall because tool data alone can be stale or miscounted.

signal.check: A research tool shows search volume with zero matching listings for a phrase, but the phrase has not been searched live on Amazon.

expected_effect.size: example: a phrase showed 1,200+ monthly searches with zero matching listings at the time checked

risk.note: None; a validation step before committing to a product bet on a keyword gap.

steps: Set the title density filter to zero in the research tool to find a candidate gap phrase.
Search that exact phrase live on Amazon.
Confirm no purpose-built listing already serves it.
Cross-check the direction with a general search-trend tool, understanding that is not proof of Amazon purchase intent.

test.method: Track whether products launched against a validated gap sold better than ones based on tool data alone.

title: Cross-check any tool revenue estimate against BSR and a sales estimator before trusting it
hypothesis: If we cross-check a research tool's revenue estimate against Best Seller Rank and a separate sales estimator, then bad go/no-go decisions fall because a single tool's modelled number can be wrong.

signal.check: A product decision is being made on one tool's revenue estimate with no cross-check against BSR or another estimator.

expected_effect.size: unknown, all such figures are modelled, not measured

risk.note: None; a cross-check step, treating all such numbers as modelled estimates.

steps: Note the revenue estimate from the primary research tool.
Check the same product's Best Seller Rank.
Run the BSR through a separate sales estimator.
Treat the numbers as a modelled range, not a fact, in the product screen sheet.

test.method: Track how close the estimated revenue range was to actual sales after launch, if the brand later sells a similar product.

title: Use giftability as a tie-breaker only, never as a gate, between two similar candidates
hypothesis: If we use giftability only to break a tie between two otherwise similar candidates, then Q4 upside is captured without over-weighting a seasonal-only product as a first launch.

signal.check: Two similar product candidates remain after screening and giftability has not been used to decide between them.

expected_effect.size: presenter estimate: Q4 volume about 3x normal for a giftable, evergreen product

risk.note: None; giftability is a tie-breaker, not a reason to accept an otherwise weaker candidate.

steps: Check whether each remaining candidate works for several occasions plus self-purchase.
Use this only to break a tie between two candidates that already passed every other gate.
Never let giftability alone override a failed price, margin or differentiation gate.

test.method: Track Q4 sales lift for launched products with and without a giftability angle.

title: Run reverse-ASIN keyword research on 2 to 3 competitor ASINs to find phrases they miss
hypothesis: If we run reverse-ASIN keyword research on top competitor ASINs, then keyword coverage improves because it surfaces the exact phrases driving their sales, including ones their own title misses.

signal.check: The listing's keyword set was built without running reverse-ASIN research on the closest competitor ASINs.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a research technique, not a measured result

risk.note: None; a research step.

prerequisites: a keyword research tool with reverse-ASIN capability
steps: Pick 2 to 3 of the closest-selling competitor ASINs.
Pull their full keyword list through reverse-ASIN lookup.
Note phrases driving their sales that the brand's own draft title and bullets miss.
Add relevant, true phrases to the keyword bucket.

test.method: Track organic clicks and rank for the added phrases after listing update.

title: Cross-check Amazon autocomplete suggestions against revenue data as an extra keyword source
hypothesis: If we type core product terms into Amazon's search box and cross-check the autocomplete suggestions against revenue data, then keyword coverage improves because autocomplete reflects real shopper phrasing the research tool may miss.

signal.check: The keyword set for a listing has not been cross-checked against Amazon's own autocomplete suggestions.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a research technique, not a measured result

risk.note: None; a research step.

steps: Type the product's core term stems into Amazon's search box.
Note every autocomplete suggestion.
Cross-check each suggestion's revenue potential in the research tool's estimator.
Add relevant, true suggestions to the keyword bucket.

test.method: Track organic clicks for autocomplete-sourced phrases after listing update.

title: Set a 30% or higher net margin gate after landed cost and all Amazon fees before launching any SKU
hypothesis: If we require 30% or more net margin after landed cost and every Amazon fee before launching, then unprofitable launches fall because this is the single largest predictor of a viable SKU across sources.

signal.check: A SKU is being considered for launch without a computed net margin after every fee line.

expected_effect.size: 30% or more net margin, 2 sources agree

risk.note: None; this is a go/no-go gate before spending on stock.

steps: Pull landed cost per unit and target sell price.
List every Amazon fee line: referral, FBA, storage, labelling, prep, returns, PPC.
Compute net margin as (price minus all costs and fees) divided by price.
Do not launch if net margin is under 30%; cut cost, raise price, or stop.

test.method: Recompute net margin from actual settlement data after the first full month of sales.

title: Price at 3x or more the unit manufacturing cost, and consider premium over cheapest positioning
hypothesis: If we price at 3x or more the unit manufacturing cost instead of racing to the lowest price, then margin after referral and fulfilment fees holds because those fees alone can take about a third of a low multiple's price.

signal.check: The planned sell price is under 3x the unit manufacturing cost.

expected_effect.size: referral plus pick and pack take about a third of price at low multiples, closer to 20-25% for pricier light items

risk.note: Premium positioning must be earned by real differentiation, not assumed as a universal strategy.

steps: Compute the price to unit-cost ratio for the planned price.
Raise price or cut unit cost if the ratio is under 3x.
Consider premium positioning only where the product has a real, provable differentiator.

test.method: Track net margin at the chosen price ratio after the first settlement cycle.

title: Model the full Amazon fee stack line by line before committing to stock
hypothesis: If we model every fee line (referral, FBA, storage, labelling, prep, returns, plan fee, duty, freight, bond) before ordering stock, then margin surprises after launch fall because no single fee line is missed or guessed.

signal.check: A margin estimate for a SKU is based on only 1 or 2 fee lines instead of the full stack.

expected_effect.size: unknown, avoids missing a fee line that erases margin

risk.note: None; a modelling step. Every fee figure needs a live check before use.

steps: List every fee line: referral, FBA pick and pack, monthly storage, long-term storage risk, labelling, prep, returns and disposal, plan fee, PPC per unit, inbound freight, duty, customs bond, VAT where it applies.
Get a live figure for each line from the fee calculator or a current web check.
Sum all lines against price to get net margin.
Flag any line still a guess rather than a live figure.

test.method: Compare the modelled fee total against the actual settlement report after the first month.

title: Compute monthly storage cost from cubic feet and the live per-cubic-foot rate, not guesswork
hypothesis: If we compute storage cost from measured cubic feet times the live rate times months in the warehouse, then the margin model reads correctly because guessed storage costs are a common source of error.

signal.check: Storage cost in the margin model is an estimate rather than calculated from measured cubic feet and the live rate.

expected_effect.size: example: a 3x4x5 inch unit is 60 cubic inches, about $0.026 per unit per month at a $0.75 rate

risk.note: None; a calculation fix.

steps: Measure the packed unit's length, width and height in inches.
Divide by 1,728 to get cubic feet.
Multiply by the live per-cubic-foot storage rate and the expected months in the warehouse.
Use the higher Q4 rate for October to December.

test.method: Compare the calculated storage cost against the actual storage fee charged.

title: Design packaging to the smallest FBA size tier that still protects the product
hypothesis: If we design packaging to fit the smallest FBA size tier that still protects the product, then per-unit fulfilment fees fall because a small-standard tier costs meaningfully less than large-standard.

signal.check: Packaging dimensions have not been checked against the size tier boundary before finalising the design.

expected_effect.size: example: small-standard saved about $0.64 per unit vs large-standard in one case

risk.note: None; a packaging design check before the production run.

steps: Check the live size and weight limits for small-standard vs large-standard.
Design packaging to fit inside the smaller tier if it still protects the product.
Confirm the final packed dimensions before ordering packaging in bulk.

test.method: Compare per-unit fulfilment fee against the size tier the final packaging landed in.

title: Read the monthly Amazon P&L by fee line, never by revenue alone
hypothesis: If we read the monthly P&L broken into revenue, product cost, referral, FBA, storage, inbound, PPC, subscription, returns and net, then real profitability shows because revenue alone hides fee creep and a stockout month.

signal.check: The brand is only checking total Amazon revenue each month, without a fee-line breakdown.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a reporting discipline change

risk.note: None; a reporting change.

steps: Pull settlement data for the month.
Break it into revenue, product cost, referral, FBA pick and pack, storage, inbound, PPC, subscription, returns, other, net.
Read net, not revenue, as the health signal.
Flag a stockout month as a stock problem, not a demand drop.

test.method: Track net margin trend month over month using the fee-line breakdown.

title: Audit Amazon's fee charges and lost or damaged inventory claims every month
hypothesis: If we audit fee charges and lost or damaged inventory every month, then recovered revenue rises because late claims may not be paid past Amazon's own escalation window.

signal.check: No monthly process exists for checking fee charges and lost or damaged inventory against what should have been charged.

expected_effect.size: escalation guidance: about a 2-week threshold outside Q4 in one source

risk.note: None; a monthly audit, no downside.

steps: Pull the month's fee charges and compare to the expected fees from the margin model.
Check the FBA Inventory Breakdown and Reimbursements report for lost or damaged units.
File a claim for any discrepancy before Amazon's stated escalation window closes.
Log recovered amounts against the audit.

test.method: Track dollars recovered per month through this audit.

title: Set the PPC budget from cost per click, conversion rate and margin, keeping a launch reserve
hypothesis: If we set the PPC budget from expected cost per click, conversion rate and unit margin instead of a flat number, then launch PPC lasts through the ramp because it matches what the funnel can actually spend.

signal.check: The PPC budget for launch is a round number chosen without reference to CPC, conversion rate or unit margin.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a budget-sizing method; keep at least about $1,000 as a launch reserve per one source

risk.note: None; a budgeting method.

steps: Estimate CPC for the target keywords.
Estimate landing conversion rate from the listing.
Compute the acceptable cost per acquisition from unit margin.
Size the launch PPC budget to sustain that spend for the launch window, with a reserve.

test.method: Compare actual CPC and conversion against the estimates used to size the budget.

title: Keep the Amazon price at or above the brand's own DTC price unless a different price is deliberately modelled
hypothesis: If we keep the Amazon price at or above the brand's DTC price unless the fee stack justifies a deliberate difference, then combined channel margin holds because undercutting the brand's own site trains buyers to wait for the cheaper channel.
does_not_apply_when: the fee stack has been modelled and a different price is a deliberate, margin-checked decision

signal.check: The Amazon price for a SKU the brand also sells on its own site is lower than the DTC price with no fee-stack reasoning behind it.

expected_effect.size: unknown, general practice

risk.note: None; a pricing consistency check across channels.

steps: Compare the Amazon price to the brand's own DTC price for the same SKU.
If Amazon is cheaper, check whether that gap is a deliberate, fee-modelled decision.
If not deliberate, raise the Amazon price to match or exceed DTC.

test.method: Track combined blended margin across DTC and Amazon after aligning price.

title: Confirm a factory's maximum monthly output before setting a launch date
hypothesis: If we confirm the factory's maximum monthly output before setting a launch date, then stockout losses fall because a fast PPC ramp or rank jump cannot outrun a manufacturer that was never asked its ceiling.

signal.check: A launch date is being set without asking the manufacturer for its maximum monthly production capacity.

expected_effect.size: one reported case: an unasked capacity limit led to an estimated $20,000+ loss

risk.note: None; a question to ask before committing to a launch date.

steps: Ask the manufacturer its maximum monthly output at full capacity.
Compare that ceiling to the sales velocity the launch plan is targeting.
Set the launch date and reorder plan so demand never outruns that ceiling.

test.method: Track stockout days against the confirmed capacity ceiling after launch.

title: Pay for a printed sample and approve it against the product brief before the FBA-bound run
hypothesis: If we pay for a printed, packaging-accurate sample and approve it against the product brief before ordering the FBA-bound run, then bad-review-driving defects fall because a defect that reaches FBA becomes a public review, not a private return.

signal.check: A production order is planned using only an off-the-shelf sample, without a paid printed sample matching final packaging.

expected_effect.size: printed sample about $200 to $300 vs off-the-shelf shipping-only cost

risk.note: Skipping this step risks shipping defects straight into FBA, which becomes a public review problem.

prerequisites: product brief with fixes from review mining
steps: Order and pay for a printed, packaging-accurate sample from the chosen factory.
Compare it against the product brief's fixes from competitor review mining.
Approve or send back for changes before placing the bulk production order.

test.method: Track the defect rate and review complaints of launches that used a paid printed sample vs those that skipped it.

title: Run a third-party inspection, including a barcode scan, before releasing the balance payment
hypothesis: If we run a paid third-party inspection with a barcode scan before releasing the balance on a bulk order, then costly returns and bad reviews fall because an uninspected defect becomes a review problem once it reaches FBA.

signal.check: A bulk production order is being paid in full, or the balance released, before a third-party inspection has confirmed quality and scanned the FNSKU and UPC.

expected_effect.size: one reported case: an uninspected run cost about $10,000 in returns and bad reviews

risk.note: None; the inspection cost is small next to the cost of a defective FBA-bound run.

steps: Pay about 30% upfront on the bulk order.
Book a third-party inspection before the balance is due.
Confirm the inspector checks unit quality against the approved sample and scans the FNSKU and UPC barcodes.
Release the balance only after a passing inspection report.

test.method: Track return rate and review complaints on inspected vs any uninspected historical runs.

title: Pay new Amazon-bound suppliers by a reversible method until trust is established
hypothesis: If we pay a new supplier by a reversible payment method until trust is established, then loss from a bad or defective run falls because a dispute has no recourse once goods are checked into an Amazon warehouse.
does_not_apply_when: the supplier relationship is already established and trusted

signal.check: A new manufacturer relationship is paying by an irreversible method (wire transfer) for the first orders.

expected_effect.size: reversible methods carry about a 3% fee in one source

risk.note: Reversible payment methods cost more in fees but protect against a run with no recourse once it reaches FBA.

steps: Check whether the supplier is new or unproven.
Use a reversible payment method (for example a card or an escrow-backed platform) rather than a wire transfer for early orders.
Move to standard terms once several clean orders build trust.

test.method: Track disputes or losses recovered on reversible-method orders vs irreversible ones.
test.read_point: on each new supplier's first orders

title: Print the FNSKU barcode on the packaging at the factory; never let Amazon apply the label
hypothesis: If we print the FNSKU on the packaging at the factory instead of letting Amazon label units, then per-unit labelling cost falls because Amazon's own labelling fee runs $0.30 to $0.50 per unit (38p in the UK).

signal.check: Units are being sent to FBA without a printed FNSKU, defaulting to Amazon's own labelling service.

expected_effect.size: $0.30 to $0.50 per unit saved (38p in the UK)

risk.note: None; a labelling method choice.

steps: Generate the FNSKU for the ASIN in Seller Central.
Send the barcode file to the factory to print directly on the packaging, or label in-house before shipping.
Select 'units already labelled' on the inbound shipment plan, never 'Amazon labels'.

test.method: Track per-unit labelling cost against the Amazon labelling fee avoided.

title: Choose air or sea freight against the launch date and PPC budget already committed, not cost alone
hypothesis: If we choose air or sea freight based on the launch date and PPC budget already committed instead of cost alone, then wasted ad spend falls because a late sea shipment means a live, advertised listing burning cash with no stock.

signal.check: A freight mode decision is being made on landed cost alone, without checking it against the committed launch date and PPC start.

expected_effect.size: example: about $11 per unit air vs about $7.50 sea for the same product

risk.note: A late sea shipment against a fixed launch date and running PPC can burn cash with no stock to sell.

steps: Check the committed launch date and any PPC spend already scheduled to start.
Model landed cost and transit time for both air and sea on the actual order size.
Choose air for a fixed, urgent launch date or a first-time import; sea for a flexible date and larger volume; split if part of the order is urgent.
Use a freight forwarder for sea shipments.

test.method: Track whether stock arrived before the committed launch date and PPC start.

title: Source consumable or ingested products domestically unless the overseas regulatory path is confirmed
hypothesis: If we source a consumable or ingested product domestically unless the overseas regulatory path is confirmed, then compliance delay and rejection risk falls because food and supplement rules vary sharply by import country.
does_not_apply_when: product is not consumable or ingested

signal.check: A consumable or ingested product is being sourced overseas without a confirmed regulatory and labelling path for import.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no source explains the regulatory reasoning, verify with a live check

risk.note: Getting this wrong can mean a rejected shipment or a compliance flag on the listing; verify with a regulatory check or counsel.

prerequisites: web check on import and labelling rules for the product and destination
steps: Check current import, labelling and safety rules for the product category and destination.
If the regulatory path overseas is unclear or unconfirmed, source the product domestically instead.
Keep documentation (Certificate of Analysis and similar) ready before listing.

test.method: Track whether the product clears compliance flags without delay after listing.

title: Put the number one target keyword phrase as the first 2 words of the title and the first bullet
hypothesis: If we front-load the number one target keyword phrase in the first 2 words of the title and bullet 1, then organic search rank and click-through improve because Amazon and shoppers both weight the front of the title most.
does_not_apply_when: the brand name is already famous enough that shoppers search it directly

signal.check: The listing title or first bullet opens with the brand name or a generic word instead of the target keyword phrase.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source_claim from listing structure guidance

risk.note: None; a copy edit to the listing.

prerequisites: keyword bucket 1 confirmed (see keyword bucket idea)
steps: Confirm the number one target keyword phrase from bucket 1.
Rewrite the title to open with that phrase.
Rewrite bullet 1 to open with the same phrase, then the core benefit.

test.method: Track organic rank and click-through rate for the target phrase after the edit.

title: Sort keywords into 3 buckets (core, supporting, buzzwords to cut) and use only the first 2
hypothesis: If we sort candidate keywords into core exact phrases, true supporting attributes, and buzzwords to cut, then listing relevance improves because generic buzzwords dilute the phrases that actually drive search matches.

signal.check: The listing's keyword list mixes core phrases, attributes and generic buzzwords with no bucketing.

expected_effect.size: example: kept 'organic', 'blood sugar', 'caffeine-free'; cut 'wellness', 'detox', 'energy', 'antioxidant-rich blend'

risk.note: None; a keyword organisation step.

steps: List every candidate keyword from research.
Sort into bucket 1 (core exact phrases), bucket 2 (true supporting attributes) and bucket 3 (generic buzzwords).
Use only bucket 1 and 2 in the title, bullets, description and backend terms.
Drop bucket 3 entirely.

test.method: Track organic clicks for the listing before and after removing bucket 3 buzzwords.

title: Write 5 listing bullets that lead with a benefit and carry one true, specific claim each
hypothesis: If we write 5 bullets that lead with a benefit and each carry one true, specific claim, then conversion improves because benefit-led, specific copy reads better than a feature list and never risks an invented claim.

signal.check: The listing's bullets are feature-led, vague, or contain a claim not on the brand's approved claims list.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source_claim on copy structure

risk.note: Never include a claim not on the brand's approved list; check the current return policy wording before any guarantee bullet.

steps: Pull the brand's approved claims list.
Write 5 bullets, each opening with a benefit.
Attach one true, specific claim from the approved list to each bullet.
Remove any vague or unapproved claim.

test.method: Track conversion rate before and after the bullet rewrite.

title: Make the main listing image differentiate the product on the search grid
hypothesis: If we make the main image a clean, high-contrast hero shot of the real product, then click-through from the search grid improves because it must win the click before any copy is read.

signal.check: The main listing image is cluttered, low-contrast, or does not clearly show the real product at thumbnail size.

expected_effect.size: example: black packaging with high-contrast red text against pale competitors stood out on the grid

risk.note: Use the real product photo; a generated image can redraw the product inaccurately.

steps: Photograph the real product against a clean, high-contrast background.
Check how the image reads at small thumbnail size on the search grid.
Remove clutter, excess packaging or logo dominance from the frame.
Replace any DIY or generated main image with a professional real-product shot.

test.method: Track click-through rate from search results before and after the image change.

title: Use all secondary image slots, including at least one comparison chart
hypothesis: If we fill all available secondary image slots including a comparison chart, then conversion improves because a listing with 4 or fewer images or DIY photos is a documented weakness signal against fuller competitor listings.

signal.check: The listing uses 4 or fewer secondary images, or DIY-quality photos, instead of the full available slots.

expected_effect.size: one source reports over $10,000 lost from poor launch images in one case

risk.note: Use real product photos; do not rely on generated images where accuracy matters.

steps: Plan secondary images for use in context, scale, packaging contents, a comparison chart against alternatives, and key benefits as text overlays.
Fill all available secondary image slots.
Replace any DIY or low-quality photo before launch.

test.method: Track conversion rate before and after completing the secondary image set.

title: Fill every listing attribute field correctly, especially shelf life and units per sellable unit
hypothesis: If we fill every attribute field correctly, especially expireable status, shelf life in days, units per sellable unit and category, then downstream errors fall because these fields control storage handling and search placement.

signal.check: One or more required attribute fields (shelf life, units per sellable unit, category, expireable status) are blank or guessed on the listing.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source_claim on listing field accuracy

risk.note: None; a listing accuracy check. Check a comparable competitor's category node if unsure.

steps: List every required attribute field for the product's category.
Fill expireable status and shelf life in days accurately for consumables.
Fill units per sellable unit and the specific category node.
Cross-check an uncertain field against a comparable competitor's listing.

test.method: Track whether the listing passes the listing audit checklist on attribute fields.
test.read_point: at listing creation and each audit

title: Fill backend search terms with leftover true keywords not already visible in the listing
hypothesis: If we fill backend search terms with true bucket 2 and 3 leftovers not already visible in the title, bullets or description, then organic search coverage improves because backend terms capture matches without cluttering visible copy.

signal.check: Backend search terms are empty, duplicated from visible copy, or missing true leftover keywords.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source_claim on backend keyword completeness

risk.note: None; a listing completeness check.

prerequisites: keyword buckets assigned to title, bullets and description
steps: List keywords not already visible in the title, bullets or description.
Confirm each is true of the product.
Enter them into the backend search terms field, avoiding duplication of visible copy.

test.method: Track organic clicks after filling backend terms.

title: Set a future offer start date so launch traffic never lands on an out-of-stock listing
lever: launch date sequencing on the listing
hypothesis: If we set the listing's offer start date to the planned launch day, then wasted launch traffic falls because the listing otherwise goes live with zero stock and no ability to convert visitors.

signal.check: The listing is built and ready but the offer start date is unset or already live before stock and PPC are ready.

expected_effect.size: unknown, sequencing check

risk.note: None; a listing setting.

steps: Confirm the planned launch date and that stock will be checked in by then.
Set the listing's offer start date to that launch date in the attributes.
Confirm the listing stays dark (not live for sale) until that date.

test.method: Confirm no orders or traffic land on the listing before the set start date.

title: Build a new listing for an own-brand product; join an existing ASIN only if resellers already listed it
hypothesis: If we build a brand-new listing for an own-brand product and only join an existing ASIN when resellers already created one, then listing control and brand presentation improve because the reseller join path is built for arbitrage, not own-brand sellers.

signal.check: A decision is being made on whether to create a new listing or join an existing ASIN, without checking whether the product already has one from a reseller.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a sequencing decision

risk.note: If resellers already listed the product, Brand Registry gives the brand control of the detail page once enrolled.

steps: Search Amazon for the exact product to check for an existing ASIN.
If none exists, build a new listing (P8).
If resellers already created one, join it and use Brand Registry to take control of the detail page.
Ignore reseller-specific advice like pricing to the lowest FBA seller; that does not apply to an own-brand seller.

test.method: Confirm the listing shows the brand as the controlling seller within 15 minutes of joining, or as expected for a new listing.

title: Plan buffer time for compliance flags on supplements, diet claims or anything a scanner may misread
hypothesis: If we plan buffer time for a possible compliance flag on supplements, diet-adjacent products or scanner-sensitive keywords, then launch delay surprises fall because these categories are reported to trigger review holds.

signal.check: A launch date is set for a supplement, diet-adjacent, or similarly sensitive product with no buffer time for a compliance flag.

expected_effect.size: example: an electrolyte product needed a Certificate of Analysis after a false 'diet product' flag

risk.note: None; a scheduling buffer.

steps: Check the live category compliance triggers for the product type.
Prepare any likely-needed document (Certificate of Analysis or similar) in advance.
Add buffer days to the launch timeline for a possible review hold.

test.method: Track days lost to compliance flags against the buffer planned.

title: Use A+ content and a listing or index checker once Brand Registered
hypothesis: If we build A+ content and run a listing or index checker once Brand Registered, then conversion and search visibility improve because A+ adds rich content and an index check confirms core phrases are actually searchable.
does_not_apply_when: brand is not yet Brand Registered

signal.check: The brand is Brand Registered but has not built A+ content or checked whether core keywords are indexed.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source names the tools but gives no step-by-step or measured result

risk.note: None; an enhancement once eligible.

steps: Build A+ content modules once Brand Registry approves.
Run a listing or index checker to confirm core keyword phrases are indexed.
Fix and re-check any phrase that is not indexed.

test.method: Track conversion rate and indexed keyword count before and after adding A+ content.

title: Mine adjacent, non-competitor listings outside the exact subcategory for attribute keyword terms
hypothesis: If we mine adjacent listings outside the exact subcategory for attribute terms, then keyword coverage improves because relevant attribute phrases (material, use case) often live in a neighbouring category's listings.

signal.check: Keyword research has only looked at direct competitors in the exact subcategory, not adjacent categories.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a research technique

risk.note: None; a research step.

steps: Identify adjacent, non-competing categories that share attributes with the product.
Read listings in those categories for true attribute terms (material, use case, audience).
Add any true, relevant term to the appropriate keyword bucket.

test.method: Track organic clicks for adjacent-sourced attribute terms after the listing update.

title: Choose a specific, accurate category node instead of accepting a too-generic auto-suggestion
hypothesis: If we browse to a specific, accurate category node instead of accepting a generic auto-suggested one, then search placement and applicable attribute fields improve because a too-generic node misses relevant attributes and search filters.

signal.check: The listing is using an auto-suggested category node that is more generic than the product's actual specific category.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a listing setup step

risk.note: None; a category selection fix.

steps: Check the auto-suggested category node during listing creation.
Browse the category tree for a more specific, accurate node.
Copy a comparable competitor's category node if unsure which is correct.

test.method: Track search placement and attribute completeness after correcting the category node.

title: Build every shipment from measured case dimensions and weight against the hard FBA size limits
hypothesis: If we build the shipment plan from measured case dimensions and weight instead of estimates, then rejected or reflowed shipments fall because the size and weight limits are hard constraints, not guidelines.

signal.check: A shipment plan is being built from estimated, not measured, case dimensions and weight.

expected_effect.size: US example: no case side over 25 inches, case under 50 lb

risk.note: None; a measurement step before booking the shipment.

steps: Measure the actual packed case length, width, height and weight.
Check against the live case limits for the target marketplace.
Repack or split the shipment if any case exceeds the limit.

test.method: Track shipment rejections or repack requests against measured vs estimated cases.

title: Save a case-pack template after the first shipment so repeat shipments reuse the same counts
hypothesis: If we save a case-pack template after the first shipment, then time spent building repeat shipments falls because the same counts and dimensions do not need re-measuring each time.

signal.check: Each new shipment for the same SKU is built from scratch instead of a saved template.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a time-saving step

risk.note: None; a template save.

prerequisites: a completed first shipment for the SKU
steps: Complete the first shipment with measured case dimensions and unit counts.
Save the case-pack template in Seller Central for that SKU.
Reuse the template for every reorder shipment of the same SKU.

test.method: Track time to build a shipment plan before and after saving the template.

title: Check every box label against the carrier label before dispatch
hypothesis: If we check every box's weight, dimensions and ship-from/ship-to against the carrier label before dispatch, then lost or misrouted shipments fall because a mismatch is a reported cause of significant lost sales.

signal.check: Boxes are being handed to the carrier without checking the printed label against the carrier's label and the shipment plan.

expected_effect.size: one reported case: a wrong ship-from address cost about $5,000 in lost sales

risk.note: None; a pre-dispatch check.

steps: Print box labels (and pallet labels for LTL) from Seller Central.
Compare weight, dimensions, ship-from and ship-to on each label against the carrier label and the shipment plan.
Note that Amazon may split a shipment across multiple fulfilment centres.
Fix any mismatch before handover.

test.method: Track shipment discrepancies or delays traced back to a label mismatch.

title: Always use the true ship-from address on every FBA shipment; never a false one
hypothesis: If we always use the true origin address on every FBA shipment, then account and shipment risk falls because entering a false address to influence fulfilment-centre assignment breaches Amazon's terms.

signal.check: A shipment plan is using a false or steering ship-from address instead of the true origin.

expected_effect.size: one source describes this as against Amazon's rules with no card support

risk.note: None; use the true address. If inbound cost matters, use a real forwarder or prep centre as the legitimate ship-from instead.

steps: Enter the true origin address for every shipment.
If inbound freight cost is a concern, route the question to sourcing for a real coastal forwarder or prep centre as a legitimate ship-from, not a false address.

test.method: Confirm every shipment plan uses a verifiable true origin address.

title: Use small parcel for boxes and LTL pallets for larger volumes
hypothesis: If we use small parcel through the partnered carrier rate for boxes and switch to LTL pallets once volume justifies it, then freight cost falls because repeated small-parcel sends can cost roughly double LTL for the same volume.

signal.check: A shipment of pallet-level volume is being sent as repeated small parcel boxes instead of LTL.

expected_effect.size: LTL can roughly halve freight cost versus repeated small parcel sends at volume

risk.note: LTL needs a trucking company, palletising, wrapping and a Bill of Lading; confirm the factory or warehouse can palletise and load a truck.

steps: Estimate the shipment's total volume and weight.
Use small parcel through the partnered carrier rate for a handful of boxes.
Switch to LTL with a freight quote once the shipment reaches 1 or more pallets.
Confirm palletising capability before booking LTL.

test.method: Compare freight cost per unit for small parcel vs LTL at the shipment's actual volume.

title: Keep every carrier receipt and Bill of Lading before handover
hypothesis: If we keep every carrier receipt and Bill of Lading before handover, then reimbursement claims succeed more often because it is the proof Amazon accepts for shipped-vs-received reconciliation.

signal.check: Shipment paperwork (carrier receipt, Bill of Lading) is not being filed and kept, especially for pallet shipments.

expected_effect.size: one reported case: a misplaced Bill of Lading nearly cost $10,000

risk.note: None; a filing habit.

steps: Collect the carrier receipt and Bill of Lading at every handover, especially pallet shipments.
File them against the shipment ID in a shared, backed-up location.
Attach them to any reimbursement claim for a shipped-vs-received discrepancy.

test.method: Track claim success rate for shipments with complete paperwork vs any without.
test.read_point: at each shipment and each claim

title: Book the carrier collection; a tracking number alone does not finish a shipment
hypothesis: If we book the carrier's collection or drop-off instead of stopping at a printed tracking number, then delayed pickups fall because a shipment is not actually moving until collection is scheduled.

signal.check: A shipment has a printed tracking number but no carrier collection or drop-off has been booked.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a sequencing check

risk.note: None; a booking step.

steps: Print the shipping label and note the tracking ID.
Book the carrier's scheduled collection or choose a drop-off point.
Confirm a collection window or drop-off time, not just the tracking number.

test.method: Confirm every shipment shows a booked collection or completed drop-off, not tracking-only status.

title: Read the FBA Inventory Breakdown before assuming stock is lost; escalate only past the normal window
hypothesis: If we read the FBA Inventory Breakdown before assuming stock is lost, then unnecessary escalations fall because FC transfer between warehouses is normal and only a delay past the stated check-in window needs a case.

signal.check: Stock that has not appeared as sellable yet is being treated as lost without checking the Inventory Breakdown status first.

expected_effect.size: check-in typically 1 to 2 weeks outside Q4, up to a month in Q4, before escalating

risk.note: None; a status-reading step before opening a case.

steps: Open Manage All Inventory and the FBA Inventory Breakdown.
Check whether units are in FC transfer, FC processing, or customer order status.
Wait through the normal check-in window (1 to 2 weeks outside Q4, up to a month in Q4) before escalating.
Open a reimbursement case with proof only past that window.

test.method: Track how many cases opened before the normal window turned out to be a false alarm.

title: Answer every dangerous-goods and prep question accurately, and set the right prep category
hypothesis: If we answer every dangerous-goods and prep question accurately and set the correct prep category, then shipment holds fall because a guessed answer can trigger a compliance hold or a mis-prepped unit.

signal.check: Dangerous-goods or prep questions on an inbound shipment are being answered by guess rather than checked against the product.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a compliance accuracy check

risk.note: None; an accuracy check on an existing required step.

steps: Check the product's true composition and packaging against the dangerous-goods questionnaire.
Set the correct prep category for fragile, liquid, adult or baby items.
For multipacks, label the poly bag, not each individual unit.

test.method: Track shipment holds or prep-related issues before and after this check.

title: Concentrate genuine sales into launch day and the first weeks, with stock live and PPC on
hypothesis: If we concentrate genuine sales into launch day and the first weeks with stock live and PPC running, then early rank and momentum improve because click-through, reviews and sales velocity are believed to drive rank in this window.
does_not_apply_when: adding a SKU to an already-proven catalogue, where launch concentration matters less

signal.check: A launch date is set but stock, PPC and audience assets are not all confirmed ready for that exact day.

expected_effect.size: presenter's best result about 75 reviews in week 1; velocity is a hypothesis, not confirmed

risk.note: Use only genuine demand; the source's own card marks launch velocity as a hypothesis, not a confirmed ranking factor, and never manufacture sales.

prerequisites: listing built with a future offer date
